summary: Describes a method for combining the congestion control of several RTP sessions from the same sender that share a bottleneck, improving delay, loss, and fairness. It aims to be simple and need few changes in applications, and says how to apply it to NADA.

plainLanguage.summary: If you send several streams down one narrow pipe, they should share it politely. This has them cooperate rather than fight each other.

questions: how do multiple rtp streams share bandwidth fairly
can several media streams cooperate to reduce delay
subtitle: Multiple media streams share a network bottleneck fairly by cooperating.

tldr.problem: When multiple RTP streams from the same sender share a network bottleneck, each one independently adjusts its rate, causing them to compete inefficiently and create unnecessary queuing delays and packet loss.
tldr.mechanism: A Flow State Exchange (FSE) collects desired rates from all flows, detects which flows share a bottleneck, and distributes the available bandwidth according to flow priorities rather than letting each flow optimise separately.
tldr.outcome: Flows can cooperate to reduce delay, lower loss, and achieve fairer bandwidth allocation. This is an experimental mechanism presented for evaluation; implementation is simpler than earlier approaches like the Congestion Manager.

today: RFC 8699 is Experimental. It defines a mechanism for research and testing, not yet deployed in production. The authors call for experimental implementations, preferably in WebRTC browsers and other RTP applications, to confirm the simulation results on real networks and report findings in Internet-Drafts.

sections.title: The Problem of Multiple Competing Streams
sections.content: When a single host sends multiple RTP media streams (for example, a video call with both audio and video) over the same network link, each stream's congestion controller works independently. Each one increases its sending rate until it sees packets drop or become marked by the network, then decreases. Since they all do this at nearly the same time, they overshoot the link capacity together, creating bursts of queue buildup and loss. The RFC compares this to the Congestion Manager, an earlier system that solved the problem by having one global controller for all flows—but that required major changes to existing applications.
sections.plainLanguage: If several people walk through a doorway without talking to each other, they bump into each other and pile up. A coordination system lets them signal so fewer collisions happen.

sections.title: Architecture: The Flow State Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC defines three components. The Shared Bottleneck Detection (SBD) watches which flows go through the same link and labels them with a Flow Group Identifier (FGI). The Flow State Exchange (FSE) is a record-keeping module that each flow updates when its congestion controller calculates a new rate. Every flow reports both the rate it calculated and (if known) how much data the application has to send. The FSE uses these inputs to compute a new rate for each flow, respecting user-specified priorities and application limits, then sends those rates back to the flows.

The whole system runs on the sender side only. Implementations can live inside one application, in a separate process that multiple applications talk to, or even in the kernel. The key requirement is that all coupled flows must use the same algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: One person acts as the coordinator, keeping track of everyone's plans and telling each person when it's their turn to go.

sections.title: Rate Distribution Algorithms
sections.content:
The RFC presents two worked examples. The Active FSE algorithm is the simplest: every time a flow updates, the FSE collects all the flow rates, sums them up, and then distributes that sum among flows based on their priorities. Flows that cannot use their full allocation (because the application has run out of data) get less, and that leftover goes to other flows. Simulation shows this does not reduce delay as much as hoped.

The Conservative Active FSE modifies the first algorithm: when a flow detects congestion and decreases its rate, the FSE proportionally reduces everyone's rate rather than letting others jump up. A timer prevents flows from reacting too quickly to the shared reduction. Simulations indicate this version reduces delay and loss significantly.

An Appendix describes a passive variant, where the FSE returns a rate to a single flow instead of dictating rates to all; the authors warn this can oscillate and is only experimental for testbed use.
sections.plainLanguage: Either the coordinator tells everyone their new speed, or each person asks the coordinator "is this speed okay?" and adjusts accordingly. The second way is trickier to get right.

sections.title: Applying the FSE to Real Congestion Control
sections.content:
The document specifies how to apply the FSE to NADA (a congestion control algorithm for WebRTC). When NADA calculates a reference rate based on feedback, the flow passes that rate to the FSE's UPDATE function instead of using it directly. The FSE replies with an adjusted rate that respects coupled flows, and NADA uses that adjusted rate for its video target rate and sending rate.

The RFC also gives guidance for applying the FSE to other algorithms, noting that receiver-side calculations (like in TCP Friendly Rate Control) may need synchronization, that stateful algorithms (like TCP window-based control) need careful consideration of state transitions, and that rate jumps (when a new flow joins) may need smoothing.
sections.plainLanguage: The congestion control algorithm sends its desired speed to the coordinator, and the coordinator sends back the actual speed it should use so everyone gets along.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Notes
sections.content:
The RFC notes that if the architecture is used across multiple applications on the same host, flows could cheat by sending false values for rate, priority, or desired rate. In the worst case, a malicious flow could prevent others from sending or make them send far too fast. However, the RFC argues this is no worse than what a UDP application could do unilaterally, so there is no new harm compared to an uncontrolled UDP sender.

On a single-user system, it is in the application author's interest to use fair priorities. On multi-user systems, applications might race to claim the highest priority; if all do, the priority system has no effect and the result is fair regardless. The RFC calls the mechanism experimental and suitable for evaluation only, pending real-world deployment experience.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad actor can lie about what they need, but the group still ends up dividing things fairly in the end if everyone is selfish in the same way.
